headline: Approved a ferry terminal at 10 Blaney Street and a Margin Street affordable housing project; continued seven other projects.
summary: Members also endorsed two lot-line plans and approved the 2027 meeting schedule. They gave the chair authority to finish a recommendation on roof-mounted wind for City Council, passed 7-1.
decisions: Continued the 57 Wharf Street and 201 Derby Street project to December 3, 2026, 8-0.
Continued the 440 Highland Avenue project to November 19, 2026, 8-0.
Continued the hotel project at 11, 5-9, and 15 Summer Street to November 19, 2026, 8-0.
Approved the C-ROD permit with changes for a new ferry terminal at 10 Blaney Street, 7-0 with one abstention.
Approved the written decision, with changes, for the Margin Street housing project, 7-0 with one abstention.
Continued the car wash proposal at 370 376 Highland Avenue to November 19, 2026, 8-0.
Endorsed the Approval Not Required plan for 6 Technology Way, 8-0.
Continued the 6,625 square foot food manufacturing building at 54-58 Swampscott Road to December 3, 2026, 8-0.
Continued the two-family home proposal at 16 Bridge Street to December 3, 2026, 8-0.
Continued changes to the 160 Federal Street site plan to November 19, 2026, 7-0 with one recusal.
Endorsed the Approval Not Required plan for 5, 7, and 9 Willson Road, 7-0 with one recusal.
Approved letting the chair finalize and send a zoning recommendation on roof-mounted wind to City Council, 7-1.
Deferred three sets of draft minutes to November 19, 2026.

D. 10 Blaney Street (Map 41, Lot 278)  
Applicant: Aaron Udy f/b/o the City of Salem  
Description: A public hearing for all persons interested in the application of 
Aaron Udy f/b/o the City of Salem located at 10 Blaney Street (Map 41, Lot 278) 
in the Industrial and Coastal Resilience Overlay District (C-ROD) for C-ROD Site 
Plan Review in accordance with Section 8.9 of the Salem Zoning Ordinance and a 
Stormwater Management Permit in accordance with Chapter 37 of the Salem 
Code of Ordinances. Specifically, the applicant proposes to construct a new ferry 
terminal building with site improvements.
City of Salem Planning Board 
Minutes November 5, 2026 
Page 4 of 20 
 
Know your rights under the Open Meeting Law M.G.L. c. 30A § 18-25 and City Ordinance § 2-2028 
through § 2-2033. 
Aaron Udy, Fennick McCredie Architecture, Daniel Collins, City of Salem Offshore 
Wind Project and Waterfront Planner, Captain Bill McHugh, City of Salem 
Harbormaster, and Deborah Fennick, Fennick McCredie.  
 
Captain McHugh shares that the current site is a double-wide trailer intended to 
be temporary and that with increased passenger ferry trips, licensed excursions, 
and passenger vessels, the temporary structure is no longer suitable. The design 
team tried to incorporate resiliency and sustainability by moving the new 
structure out of the velocity zone, increasing elevation, and assuring a tight 
building envelope without relying on fossil fuels. This will complement the 
adjoining port marshalling site.  
 
Ms. Fennick says this is an all-electric building and is intended to capture 
daylight, shading, and natural ventilation. There will be provisions for 
photovoltaic and or small wind turbines for renewable energy. The Design 
Review Board (DRB) met with the team twice and the team incorporated many 
of the DRB comments including slate siding, and a roof that can receive future 
photovoltaics.  
 
Mr. Udy discusses the existing conditions: there are one hundred and thirty 
three (133) parking spaces, and all are to remain. The current velocity zone cuts 
through the existing building, the new building will be built north of the existing. 
Connections to the offshore wind site, Harborwalk, and the neighboring marina. 
Future Derby Street connection as well. The area of work will connect to the 
existing transformer. The construction zone will allow full access for vehicles 
(fueling and emergencies) A temporary kiosk for ticket sales will be constructed 
as the project is expected to take twelve to fourteen (12-14) months.  
 
Mr. Collins discusses the 8.9.10 C-ROD criteria. Planning staff and the Building 
Commissioner agreed that this project should be reviewed under this criteria. 
The risk of flooding has been eliminated. The design flood elevation is fourteen 
point four (14.4) feet. This is the most restrictive C-ROD element in the building 
footprint. Elevating all occupied space based on 2070 floodplain. Below the 
floodplain will be salvaged granite. Mechanical and electrical services are located 
above the sea level rise base flood elevation (SLR-BFE). That can be practically 
done so.  
 
Mr. Udy says that the turning radius is forty (40) feet from the island to the curb  
and is able to be made by emergency vehicles. Pedestrian access will connect to 
the Harborwalk on the left side of lot. There will be several rooftop units, but 
there will be perforated metal screens and pipe railing hiding these mechanicals. 
Can produce sample of the screen if the Board would like. The building in the

neighborhood context: compliments but does not mimic existing architecture. It 
is a public building with a civic presence.  
 
Public Comment 
 
None 
 
Planning Board Comments 
 
Mr. Caunter happy to see progress on the ferry terminal. Interested in how the 
pedestrian pathways will be integrated into the site. Right now, it is parking 
focused. What will enhance the pedestrian experience? The building is 
underwhelming and doesn’t read nautical. Mr. Udy shares that the pedestrian 
access is a focal point.  
 
Ms. Eimert notes that she is not eligible to vote but can participate in the 
discussion. Curious if the team can speak to the existing crosswalk and if it will 
be improved or as is? Thinks a raised crosswalk would be excellent to enhance 
the site. Mr. Udy says that is a great suggestion. Mr. Rieder says the double 
guardrail is strange and sees pedestrians trip over them.  
 
Captain McHugh says that the Derby Street connector will help as well as 
working with the project next door to allow the public to be closer to the water. 
Regarding the guardrails, those were there for access. The only part for truck is 
to support fueling operations, and you have to have containment should there 
ever be a leak. That rail protects, along with angular slopes. Thinks the use of 
furniture on the Harborwalk will help to fix this. Mr. Rieder thinks a monolith 
would be better. 
 
Mr. Rieder asks about base flood v. design flood elevation. Mr. Collins says that 
C-ROD requirement is between fourteen point two and fourteen point four 
(14.2-14.4), so the most restrictive applies (fourteen point four [14.4]).They also 
used the climate resilience design standards tool which is suggested by the 
Massachusetts Office of Coastal Zone Management (CZM) and the 2070, 100 
year flood elevation was thirteen point four (13.4). CZM wants to see one point 
five (1.5) feet freeboard on top of that. It helps meets the SLR-BFE. The team is 
going for the more restrictive. Mr. Rieder asks about sculpture;  Mr. Collins says 
that it is a temporary location and the intention is move it when the building was 
built to the location shown on the rendering. Regarding the backflow preventer 
for plumbing and fire protection line; this is the clean vessel pump as well as the 
pump boat for recreation vessels and hoses will pipe below. What is the material 
on the emergency lane; existing asphalt and then concrete on the pier. Likely to
City of Salem Planning Board

through § 2-2033. 
disturb some of it with in-kind replacement. Mr. Rieder says that if it is not 
accessed regularly, it seems like a distraction to have people walk toward it. A 
change in material would be good. And less asphalt. Captain McHugh says that 
the pump needs to have a vehicle with a crane but needs to keep it accessible. 
Mr. Rieder on the railing: Why is it so white rather than silver? And there are 
missing vertical posts on one of the renderings. This would be more visually 
recessive if silver/black/ matte gray. Ms. Fennick says they will finalize that but 
that the elevated deck is to emulate the ship deck. Mr. Rieder worries about it 
looking worn quickly. Curious of they are actual ramps or inclines. Ms. Fennick 
says a combination. The lower section is a sloped walkway rather than a ramp. 
Does the reclaimed granite create a lip? Doesn’t’ want to see someone go off the 
slope.  
 
Mr. Rieder asks about DRB recommendations. Ms. Cunningham says that this 
project was not required to go to DRB so there are no recommendations. Ms. 
Tarbet says that this is close to what was discussed. There were comments about 
the orange roof (no orange and black building in Salem!).  
 
Mr. Rieder says that he notices individuals who take care of the vessels tend to 
park right in the pedestrian spaces. Captain McHugh says it is a designated port 
area and allowed If they are working on ferry, loading materials, city vehicles to 
service city boats. They are not left to park, but they are authorized. The 
pedestrian areas are not the pier. Mr. Rieder concerned there are no trees. 
Captain McHugh says that the trees are associated with the area adjacent to the 
building, along the property line with the offshore wind site. Trees in and around 
the terminal itself would impede functionality.  
 
A motion to close the public hearing is made by Josh Turiel, seconded by Jonathan Berk, and 
passes 8-0 in a roll call vote.

E. 56 Margin Street, 54 Margin Street, 7 High Street, 20 Endicott Street (Map 25, Lot 
597), 24 Endicott Street (Map 25, Lot 595)  
Applicant: Harborlight Homes and Lifebridge North Shore  
Description: A continuation of a public hearing for all persons interested in the 
application of Harborlight Homes and Lifebridge North Shore at 56, 54 Margin 
Street, 20 Endicott Street, 7 High Street (Map 25, Lot 597) and 24 Endicott Street 
(Map 25, Lot 595) in the Residential Two-Family District (R2), Coastal Resilience 
Overlay District (C-ROD), Flood Hazard Overlay District (FHOD), and Smart Growth 
Overlay District (SGOD) for Smart Growth Overlay Plan Review and Coastal 
Resilience Overlay Site Plan Review in accordance with the following sections of the 
Salem Zoning Ordinance: Section 7.4 Smart Growth Overlay District and Section 8.9 
Coastal Resiliency Overlay District. Specifically, the applicant proposes the 
demolition of the buildings at 24 Endicott Street (Map 25, Lot 595) and 56 Margin 
Street (Map 25, Lot 597), the adaptive reuse of 54 Margin Street (Map 25, Lot 597), 
and the preservation of the façade of 20 Endicott Street (Map 25, Lot 597) to 
accommodate for a 22,806 square foot building comprised of 53 affordable homes, 
a shelter with 70 beds, and supportive programing space along with other site 
improvements. Thirteen parking spaces are proposed on site. 
 
Pat Connolly and Stefano Bassos. Presenting landscape changes and DRB 
recommendations.  
 
Proposing all new street trees on Margin Street. Morton Glossy Elm. Swapped out 
arborvitae for holly and juniper. On Pratt Street, it is too tight for another tree but 
did add a planter with hydrangeas. Adding more green between the retaining wall, 
park, and building. Planning on viburnums. On the Pratt Street sidewalk, the existing 
is on the property and to accommodate the program, they propose that the building 
go to nearly the property line. There is no room on the site to create a new sidewalk.  
 
Mr. Basso says the DRB asked them to try and remove the corner boards. Concern 
that this makes the building too busy. Hardie shingles that are to look like cedar

shakes, metal trim piece to continue to be ablet to use this product which is made 
for a corner board.  
 
Public Comment 
 
Scott Morgan 
7 Savona Street 
Asks if the High Street Park is a public park or just for residents. He is concerned 
about increasing the number of unhoused individuals in Salem. 
 
Planning Board Comment 
 
Mr. Furey says that the park is getting a major renovation and thinks it will be a 
vibrant part of the neighborhood.  
 
Mr. Rieder is happy to see that the park is continuing to be a park. Asks if the chain 
link fence is existing? Mr. Connoly says they are not touching the retaining wall. 
 
Mr. Berk clarifies that the DRB asked the team to present two options but left it to 
the Planning Board to decide? Ms. Tarbet says that the DRB said to investigate and 
but left it to the Planning Board. Mr. Berk says that they were interested in massing 
breaks, which the original design does.  
 
Ms. Eimert agrees with Mr. Berk. Asks for the pinch point on the High Street 
sidewalk to be shown. The design standards are four (4) feet. Mr. Connolly says 2 
feet approximately. Ms. Eimert says the program requirements pull the envelope to 
that point, is there a way to minimize the narrowness? Mr. Connolly says they could 
remove the planter, reduce the size, etc. Ms. Eimert suggest that the Board consider 
this to make the corner more active. The intent of the project is supportive housing, 
but when people have housing, they prefer to spend time in their own homes. She 
reminds that all people are allowed to exist in public spaces.  
 
Mr. Rieder regarding the curb, this is a city issue regarding ADA access? Mr. Connolly 
says the zoning allows for a building up to 0 foot setback. Supportive of sidewalk but 
should be in the public way. Mr. Rieder says that this sidewalk is largely parked on, 
not pedestrian. Ultimately the city should make a public accessible way, the city may 
have to remove one (1) or more parking spaces to make it passable. The applicant 
has a right to their property, and the public way is the city’s responsibility.  
 
Mr. Rieder is surprised at the variety of the elm and that the landscape is not 
American elm focused. Doesn’t love all the same glossy elm on Margin Street. 
Would like to speak with the landscape architect offline. Regarding corner boards, 
simplifying makes the building less visually imposing.

Ms. Tarbet clarifies that it is replacing the trim to the trim to match the clapboards. 
Mr. Basso confirms same terminus for each material type. Ms. Tarbet is in favor of 
monochromatic with a vertical four inch trim.  
 
Mr. Furey says the Salem YMCA is adding a new addition to the roof. Right now, staff 
take the kids down to High Street park and thinks they need to think of the people 
inside the facility. Need to get this project done. Doesn’t like the micromanaging. 
Mr. Rieder says they are not delaying the project.

F. 370 376 Highland Avenue (Map 3, Lot 63) 378 380 Highland Avenue (Map 3, Lot 
64), 382 Highland Avenue (Map 3, Lot 65)  
Applicant: Joseph Correnti f/b/o GR Development LLC  
Description: A continuation of a public hearing for all persons interested in the 
application Joseph Correnti f/b/o GR Development LLC for the property located at 
370 376 Highland Avenue (Map 3, Lot 63) 378 380 Highland Avenue (Map 3, Lot 64) 
and 382 Highland Avenue (Map 3, Lot 65) in the (B2) Business Highway and (ECOD) 
Entrance Corridor Overlay District zoning districts for Site Plan Review in accordance 
with Section 9.5 of the Salem Zoning Ordinance. Specifically, the applicant proposes

to demolish two existing buildings onsite, "Puleo's Dairy" and a storage facility, to 
construct a 4,400 s.f. car wash facility. 24 onsite parking spaces are proposed, 22 of 
which will also be used as vacuum stations. 
 
Attorney Joseph Correnti, Frank Dougherty, Washville, Scott Thornton, Vanasse and 
Associates and Bob Griffin, Griffin Engineering are in attendance. 
 
Mr. Thornton shares his screen. Traffic counts were collected in June 2026. Access 
provided with three (3) curb cuts on Highland Avenue and a fourth (4th) on Savona 
Street. Savona Street is a dead end and there is no plan to extend Savona Street. The 
traffic study area: the intersection of Savona Street and Ravenna Avenue, and 
Highland Avenue and Ravenna Avenue. Highland Avenue is under MassDOT 
jurisdiction. Current projects on Highland Avenue (Walmart, Popeyes, etc.) were 
considered. Also considered the Complete Streets project running on Highland 
Avenue. One to two (1-2) cars per minute in peak hours with less other times. The 
curb cuts on Highland Avenue have been consolidated into one and pushed to the 
north of the site. Expecting full access on Savona Street and will address 
neighborhood traffic with signage. Looked at condition where Savona Street was 
only an entrance to the site. Know that this change would not impact the project. 
Will discuss Ravenna Avenue signal time with MassDOT.  
 
Public Comment 
 
Written Public Comment 
 
Scott Morgan 
7 Savona Street 
Oppose any use of Savona Street. This site has full frontage on Highland Avenue. 
This is a high turnover business. Asks the board to deny access through Savona 
Street. Asks for the following conditions if the project is approved: 1. No access to 
Savona Street or Ravenna Avenue; 2. A physical barrier at the rear to enforce this 
restriction. 3. A requirement that all customer delivery traffic use Highland Avenue 
only.  
 
Michele  Schultz 
Lives on first house on right on Ravenna Avenue. This has taken away any possible 
peace for her. Concerned about the noise and lighting pollution that will come with 
the site. Curious why this spot is good for this type of business. Don’t need a 
carwash. There is already enough traffic on Highland Avenue.
City of Salem Planning Board 
Minutes November 5, 2026 
Page 11 of 20 
 
Know your rights under the Open Meeting Law M.G.L. c. 30A § 18-25 and City Ordinance § 2-2028

Tim Flynn 
Ward 4 councilor 
42 Sable Road 
Would like the Board to take a ride around Ravenna Avenue and pay attention to 
the turn before Ravenna meets Barcelona. Most of the businesses on Highland 
Avenue enter and exit on Highland Avenue.  
 
Helen Hughes 
24 Ravenna Avenue  
Concerned about traffic on Savona and Ravenna. Could this access road be for 
emergency vehicles only?  
 
Planning Board Comment 
 
Mr. Furey says that there has been this argument before when they were building 
condos and possibly using Barcelona Avenue as a cut through to Marlborough Road. 
Thinks Highland Avenue should be the entrance and exit.  
 
Mr. Correnti clarifies that Savona Street is a public street. The entirety of the parcel 
is B2, fronts on Savona Street and it is behind Savona Street where the R1 starts. 
Asks for the opportunity to come back and address the idea of using Savona. 
Whether the street is accepted by the city or not does not determine if it can be 
used or not.  
 
Mr. Turiel says that this is a legal B2 use. His concerns are with the traffic from 
Savona Street and the potential noise.  
 
Mr. Wing thinks that the use of Savona Street is to make ease of access on the 
opposite direction to Highland Avenue. Curious if there are issues using St. Jean’s 
Credit Unit two-way exit. If there are not, how many additional trip make this a 
concern.  
 
Ms. Tarbet clarifies that the anticipation of traffic is that there are no cars taking a 
right on to Ravenna during peak times. Mr. Thronton says yes, they assume half 
traffic is from the north and the other half south. How does the analysis handle the 
idea that this will be a cut through? Mr. Thornton thinks people do it one time and 
then that is it.  
 
Mr. Rieder says it would be good to model what a fully in and out via Highland 
Avenue does to this proposal. Maybe look at two (2) curb cuts rather than one (1). 
Mr. Correnti says that the idea of using Savona Street is a traffic safety issue.  
 
A motion to continue to the November 19, 2026 regular Planning Board meeting  is made by Josh 
Turiel, seconded by Graham Wing, and passes 8-0 in a roll call vote.
